passage:
The placement cell smelled of printer ink. Vandana Ma'am held out the slip. 'Payal, you've been shortlisted. Group discussion on Thursday, then interview.'
Payal didn't take it. 'Can I... skip this one?'
'This is the third company you've skipped. And you missed the seminar marks last month.'
Payal looked at the noticeboard, at the names of classmates already placed. Last year she had topped the department. Now she ate lunch in the washroom corridor so no one would ask her anything, and she hadn't spoken in a tutorial since August.
'I'll apply off-campus,' she said. She had said that before.
Walking out, she folded the unsigned slip into a tiny square. Her face burned. It wasn't the discussion she feared most anymore; it was how much she had already let go.

qa.q: How many companies has Payal skipped, according to Vandana Ma'am?
qa.a: This is the third company Payal has skipped.

qa.q: What is Payal feeling as she folds the unsigned slip?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and disappointed in herself, her face burning at how much she has let go since topping the department.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Payal now?
qa.a: She could tell Vandana Ma'am the truth about the fear and ask for help, perhaps starting with one small practice discussion and a visit to the college counsellor, instead of skipping again.

qa.q: How might Vandana Ma'am see Payal's refusal?
qa.a: Vandana Ma'am probably sees a capable student letting chances slip and feels puzzled or concerned, noticing the pattern of skipped companies and missed seminar marks.

grounding: It shows a student declining placements and letting studies slip, ashamed that avoiding now costs more than the original fear.

passage:
Subject: sorry I went quiet
Nikita,
You asked why I didn't come to the farewell. Honest answer: I haven't been to the office in six weeks. I told my manager it's my back. It isn't.
It started with dodging client calls. Now I dodge everything. They offered me the team-lead role last month, the one we used to joke about wanting, and I said no because it means presenting every Monday. My review came back 'below expectations'. That has never happened before.
The worst part isn't the fear anymore. It's watching my own life shrink and knowing I'm the one shrinking it. I feel like I've let down the person you knew in college.
I don't know what I want you to say. I just didn't want to lie to you too.
Gautam

qa.q: What role did Gautam turn down last month?
qa.a: Gautam turned down the team-lead role.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel about the person Nikita knew in college?
qa.a: Gautam feels ashamed and disappointed, sensing that the person from college has been let down.

qa.q: What turning point might this email itself open?
qa.a: Telling Nikita the truth breaks the secrecy; a next step could be asking Nikita to help book time with a doctor or counsellor, since the avoiding now costs work and friendships.

qa.q: What might Nikita feel reading 'I just didn't want to lie to you too'?
qa.a: Nikita may feel sad at how much Gautam has carried alone, but also trusted and glad to finally understand the silence.

grounding: It shows a young adult whose avoidance has cost a promotion and a good review, leaving shame and disappointment heavier than the first fear.

passage:
September. Irawati was offered an interview for a paid summer internship at a design firm. She said she'd think about it, then let the deadline pass. The thought of a panel staring at her portfolio made her chest tight.
November. She skipped the class trip to the craft museum, then two studio critiques where she would have had to present. Her grades slipped. Irfan, her studio partner, presented their joint project alone and texted, "Missed you. Everything okay?" She replied, "Sick."
January. The internship results went up on the notice board. Irfan had got the place she'd been offered first. She congratulated him, then cried in the washroom, not from envy exactly, but from shame. She had been good enough. Her fear had simply been louder.
That night she wrote in her sketchbook: I'm missing my own life. Staying safe has cost more than the fear ever did.

qa.q: Who got the internship?
qa.a: Irfan.

qa.q: Why did Irawati cry in the washroom?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and disappointed in herself, knowing she had been good enough but let fear make her decline.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Irawati now?
qa.a: Seeing the cost, she could take one small feared step, like presenting at the next critique, and think about talking to a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel presenting the joint project alone?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt worried and a bit alone, missing his partner and unsure what was wrong.

grounding: Over months a student declines opportunities and her studies suffer, until the shame shows avoiding now costs more than the fear.

passage:
Kamal, you keep saying no to things. The college debate, the job fair, even your friend's wedding speech. Let me tell you about Siddharth at twenty.
I was terrified of speaking in front of people. So I avoided it. I told my professor I was sick on the day of my viva and took a lower grade. When my first boss offered me the chance to present to clients, I said I was busy. I stopped going to my cousins' weddings because someone might hand me the microphone.
Each time I felt relief. But by twenty-two I was stuck in the same desk job, watching less capable people move ahead. I remember sitting on the bus home one evening, so ashamed I couldn't look at my own reflection in the window. The avoiding had cost me more than any speech ever could.
That evening was the turning point. I went to a public speaking club the next week, shaking. Your turn is coming.

qa.q: What did Siddharth tell the professor on the day of the viva?
qa.a: I was sick.

qa.q: What did young Siddharth feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Young Siddharth felt deeply ashamed and disappointed, seeing that avoiding had cost more than any speech.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned things around?
qa.a: After the shameful bus ride, Siddharth chose to go to a public speaking club the next week, even while shaking.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's first boss have seen the refusals?
qa.a: The boss may have been puzzled or disappointed, reading fear as lack of interest and giving the chances to others.

grounding: An elder recalls declining chances out of fear until work suffered and shame showed that avoiding cost more than the fear.

passage:
On placement day the rain flooded the road outside the Kolkata campus, and the hostel's power was out. Arnab banged on Tarun's door at eight. "The auto's waiting. Your interview's at ten!"
Tarun was dressed, file ready. But his heart was racing and his hands were cold, the way they had been before every exam and group discussion this year. He had already skipped two company talks and a mock interview. Each time he'd felt relief, and each time the next thing felt worse.
"Go without me," he said through the door. "I'm not well."
"Tarun, it's the company you wanted."
He heard Arnab's footsteps fade. He sat on the bed listening to the rain, and the relief came, and right behind it a wave of shame so heavy he couldn't lift his head. His friends were building lives. He was building a smaller and smaller room.

qa.q: What time was Tarun's interview?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel after the relief faded?
qa.a: He felt crushing shame and disappointment, seeing his life narrow while his friends moved ahead.

qa.q: What could Tarun do after this day?
qa.a: Tell Arnab the truth, take one small feared step like a mock interview, and see a counsellor or doctor, since the fear is limiting his life.

qa.q: What might Arnab feel as he walks away?
qa.a: Arnab likely feels frustrated and worried, not understanding why his friend is missing the job he wanted.

grounding: On a rainy placement day a student skips the interview he wanted, and the relief gives way to shame as his life narrows.

passage: The email from the architecture firm in Bengaluru sat in Tenzin's inbox for nine days before he declined the internship. It would mean presenting to clients, and just picturing that made his hands go cold. In the hostel mess, his classmate Vandana waved her phone. "Did you accept? I got the Chennai office! We can compare notes!" Tenzin said he'd decided to stay back and focus on his portfolio. He hadn't opened the portfolio in weeks. He had also skipped two studio reviews this term, and his grades showed it. That evening, walking past the chai stall, he watched the same group of juniors he used to mentor laughing about their site visit. A heavy, sour feeling sat in his chest. A year ago he had wanted to be the one presenting. Now he couldn't even explain to Vandana why he'd said no.

qa.q: How long did the email from the firm sit in Tenzin's inbox?
qa.a: It sat in Tenzin's inbox for nine days before he declined.

qa.q: What is the heavy, sour feeling in Tenzin's chest?
qa.a: It is shame and disappointment in himself, because he gave up something he once wanted and cannot explain why.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Tenzin?
qa.a: He could tell Vandana or a college counsellor honestly that fear of presenting is behind the refusals, and seek help before more opportunities slip away.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Tenzin's answer about his portfolio?
qa.a: Vandana may feel puzzled and a little let down, having expected to share the excitement, and may not guess that fear is behind it.

grounding: Shows opportunities declined and study suffering as avoidance grows, leaving the young adult ashamed and disappointed in himself.
